newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Japan's EPDC eyes stake in Ensham coal mine.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Japan's EPDC eyes stake in Ensham coal mine.

text.p: Japan's Electric Power Development Co Ltd (EPDC) is negotiating to buy a 10 percent interest in the Ensham coal mine in the state of Queensland, EPDC executive managing director Haruo Tsuchida told Reuters on Tuesday.
The mine, which produces 1.8 million tonnes of thermal coal a year, is presently owned 95 percent by Japan's Idemitsu Kosan and five percent by South Korea's Lucky Goldstar.
"The intention is firm that we will participate," said the chief of Japan's largest state-owned electricity combine.
Tsuchida would not disclose the likely price because negotiations, which revolved around tax and accounting details, are continuing.

EPDC already owns seven percent of the Blair Athol steaming coal mine in Queensland, which produces about 10 million tonnes a year. Although EPDC had no definite plans to buy into further Australian coal mines, expanding Asian coal demand made further investments a possibility, he said.
Tsuchida said discussions with Australian Minister for Resources and Energy Senator Warwick Parer had produced an Australian government go-ahead for the acquisition.
Parer also told Reuters in an interview that EPDC's investment in the mine, 350 miles west of the port of Gladstone, was welcome.

Elaborating on his formal presentation at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) coal conference in the coastal town of Terrigal, north of Sydney, Tsuchida told Reuters that structural changes in the world coal market could be reflected in lower coal prices in long-term contracts.
Increasing trade is being conducted on a spot basis so it is to be expected that long-term contracts will reflect that, he said.
Spot prices are generally below long-term contract prices.

The APEC coal conference was presented during its first day with figures for big increases in Asian steam coal trade into the first decade of the next century and of huge investments planned in Australia, Indonesia and other countries to keep pace with demand.
A parallel theme in afternoon sessions concentrated on a declining real price of traded coal in recent years.
Australian speakers rejected views, such as those voiced by Tsuchida, that the changing market was likely to be accompanied by further real price falls. - Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
